Evidence Readings/When does digital growth become durable use?
Evidence Reading

When does digital growth become durable use?

Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it.

Evidence period
Provider data 2016–2019, from a 2020 study of five e-money providers
Last reviewed
26 September 2026

Do not infer: Registrations, accounts, one-time use, transaction growth and infrastructure expansion do not prove unique, repeat, voluntary or durable financial use.

By December 2019, the five e-money providers covered by a study of the Institute of Banking Studies had 807,919 electronic-money accounts. The same study reports an average dormant or inactive share of 23%, and notes that some accounts were used only once, or because circumstances required it.

This is not a paradox. The number of accounts establishes scale within the source universe. Dormancy and one-off use show why scale alone does not establish durable financial use.

Account growth is not the same as durable digital use

Analytical text alternative
  1. Analytical question: What did historical e-money growth actually establish about use?
  2. What the evidence shows: In the historical study by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS) of five electronic-money providers, accounts reached 807,919 in December 2019, with an average dormant or inactive share of 23%; the source notes that some accounts were used once or because circumstances imposed their use. A CauseWay grouping of the study's 2019 transaction values puts 57.03% in cash-in and cash-out, 29.97% in movements between bank and electronic accounts, and 2.41% in bills and purchases combined; the grouping is CauseWay's, not a source headline. Account registrations and digital activity do not, on their own, establish voluntary and sustained use: registered accounts are not unique active people, and the 2016–2019 pattern cannot be extended to national prevalence in 2026.
  3. Scope and time: 2016–2019, with account level at Dec-2019 · Five electronic-money providers in the historical study by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS); transaction-value categories limited to those in the source
  4. What not to conclude: Registered accounts are not unique active people, and the historical five-provider pattern does not show national prevalence in 2026.
2016–2019, with account level at Dec-2019Five electronic-money providers in the historical study by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS); transaction-value categories limited to those in the source

An account can exist without becoming a relationship

Registration does not tell us whether an account was used once or repeatedly, whether use was voluntary or triggered by a payment someone else made, whether value stayed in the account, whether the user paid or saved with it, or whether the service became preferable to cash for any purpose.

What the money moved for

CauseWay’s grouping of a 2019 transaction table in the same study indicates that 57.03% of recorded e-money transaction value was cash-in or cash-out and 29.97% was movement between bank and electronic accounts; bills and purchases together were 2.41%. The grouping is CauseWay’s, not a headline in the source.

Cash-in and cash-out are not failed digital finance. Where moving value safely or easily is hard, that function has real economic use. But a system dominated by entry to and exit from cash tells us something different from repeated merchant, bill, saving or other digital use.

Useful before durable

The evidence supports neither extreme: that every new account proves inclusion, or that episodic use proves digital finance failed. A service can solve a real problem once and still not become a persistent financial relationship.

The historical provider evidence also reports strong urban concentration and a low share of women within its own universe. These are not 2026 national estimates. Their present value is to show what current measurement must test: who uses digital finance, not merely how many accounts exist.

What would change this reading?

Current data on unique active users, recency and frequency of use, what accounts are used for, value retained in the account, merchant and bill payments, dormancy, failed transactions, cost, complaints and provider-side behaviour, combined with demand-side questions on why people open an account, use it, return to it or stop. The measures that matter are registration, activity, recency, frequency, function, choice or trigger, quality and persistence, and they should not be read as an automatic ladder.

Scale tells us how large the digital system became. Return use tells us whether it entered financial life.

Related readings

  • The payment arrived. What happened next?Material on Yemen’s digital-payment pilot describes transfers paid into fully functional accounts, with recipient choice, for 45,460 recipients. That is an important step in delivery. It is not yet evidence that the accounts stayed part of recipients’ financial lives after the payments.
  • When does a payment reform become financial inclusion?A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced.
